title: How do restaurants and fast-food chains make money, and what matters in their cases?
description: Restaurant economics for case interviews: covers, average spend, food and labour costs, franchising and delivery apps, with a worked unit-economics example.
hook: Restaurant cases are popular because everyone understands the product. Underneath, they test unit economics: what one restaurant earns, what it costs to run, and how chains grow through franchising.
body:
The basic equation

Revenue = covers (customers served) × average spend. The biggest costs are usually food and labour, followed by rent.

A worked example: one restaurant's profit

A fast-casual restaurant serves 400 customers a day at £10 each, 360 days a year: £1.44M revenue. If food is 30% (£432k), labour 30% (£432k), rent and other costs 25% (£360k), it keeps 15%, about £216k a year. If it cost £600k to open, payback is under three years.

Franchising

Many chains let franchisees own and run restaurants, taking a royalty on sales. The chain earns less per restaurant but grows faster with less money and risk (see business models).

Delivery apps

Apps bring orders but charge high commissions, which can turn a profitable order into a loss. The profitability guide works through exactly this problem.

Typical restaurant case questions

  • Why are profits falling despite stable sales?
  • Should we expand through franchising?
  • Should we launch a delivery-only kitchen?
outro: Next in this topic: How do online retailers make money, and what matters in an e-commerce case?
